name: Probiotics / fermented food for skin

lead: Probiotics are live microorganisms that, in the WHO's 2001 wording, confer a health benefit when given in adequate amounts. Fermented foods such as yogurt, kefir, kimchi and sauerkraut contain live cultures, and both foods and supplements are discussed in skin communities for acne and inflammation.

Wikipedia describes the use of probiotics and synbiotics for acne as preliminary research, with possible reductions in inflammatory lesions and improved barrier function. For eczema, the American Academy of Dermatology does not recommend probiotics for established atopic dermatitis.

paras: The proposed idea is a gut-skin axis in which gut bacteria influence systemic inflammation and the skin. Wikipedia notes that benefits are strain-specific and cannot be assumed across strains, and that gut-microbiome research relies heavily on animal models and small human studies.

Probiotics are generally considered safe, but rare bloodstream infections have occurred in critically ill or immunocompromised people. Common side effects at higher amounts include bloating and gas. EFSA has rejected probiotic health claims for insufficient evidence.

lead: Probiotics are live microorganisms defined by the WHO in 2001 as conferring a health benefit on the host when administered in adequate amounts; the European Food Safety Authority rejects that definition because it builds in an unmeasurable health claim [1]. Fermented foods such as yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and kombucha contain live cultures and have been eaten for centuries [1].

In skin and looksmaxxing circles, probiotic supplements and fermented foods are discussed as a way to improve acne and complexion through the gut. Wikipedia describes probiotics and synbiotics for acne as in preliminary research, noting possible reductions in inflammatory lesions and inflammatory markers [1].
Published evidence specific to fermented food and skin appearance was not located in the sources reviewed for this entry.
infobox: Yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut, probiotic capsules
EFSA has rejected probiotic health claims (as of 2019)

paras: Bulgarian physician Stamen Grigorov identified the bacterium later named Lactobacillus bulgaricus in yogurt in 1905. Around 1907 Nobel laureate Elie Metchnikoff proposed that fermented milk could seed the gut with beneficial bacteria, linking yogurt consumption to longevity [1].

Wikipedia states that a review describes probiotics and synbiotics for acne as preliminary, with possible reductions in inflammatory lesions and improved skin barrier function, while the American Academy of Dermatology does not recommend probiotics for established atopic dermatitis because evidence is inconsistent [1]. No individual trials of fermented foods such as kefir or kimchi for acne were identified.

Probiotics are generally regarded as safe, but people with immunodeficiency, short bowel syndrome, central venous catheters or cardiac valve disease, and premature infants may face higher risk, and rare bloodstream infections have been reported in critically ill or immunocompromised children [1].

EFSA had rejected all manufacturer petitions for probiotic health claims as of 2019 for insufficient evidence of cause and effect, and the US FDA has sent warning letters to makers claiming to treat disease [1].

lore.intro: Probiotic and fermented-food routines are discussed as part of gut-focused approaches to acne.

claims.claim: Probiotics, kefir or kimchi can clear acne
